analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on February 4, 2015 and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently eliminated the federal estate tax, the tax owed on estates left at death, effective for people dying after December 31, 2014. Today only estates above a high exemption level pay any estate tax, so the benefit goes almost entirely to heirs of very large fortunes. The bill would also have kept the "stepped-up basis" rule, which means capital gains on inherited assets would never be taxed at all, costing the Treasury further revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. In 2015 the estate tax applied only above roughly $5.4 million per person (about $10.9 million per couple), so only a small fraction of the largest estates owed anything; full repeal would hand those heirs a tax cut measured in the hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars per estate. Wealthy families with appreciated stock, real estate, and businesses would gain the most, since the bill also retains stepped-up basis — meaning the untaxed gain in inherited assets would escape capital gains tax entirely.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal estate tax permanently, effective for estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2014.
Retains stepped-up basis at death, so inherited assets keep a tax-free reset of their value and any lifetime capital gains in them escape tax forever.

Supporters' core argument: family-owned farms and small businesses could face pressure to sell assets to pay an estate tax bill; repeal would end that risk, though under the exemption levels in force at the time very few estates actually owed the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Repeal would permanently drain tens of billions of dollars a year in estate tax revenue from the Treasury, which must be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or smaller public services. Because the bill keeps stepped-up basis, the richest families would also avoid capital gains tax on assets they never sold during their lifetime.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would permanently eliminate revenue from a tax paid only by a small share of the very largest estates, shifting the burden to everyone else through other taxes or borrowing.

The bill keeps stepped-up basis, so capital gains on inherited assets would never be taxed — an effective zero-percent rate on the largest untaxed lifetime gains, a major leak in the tax system that repeal of the estate tax alone does not fix.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concentrated: a permanent, multi-billion-dollar-a-year tax cut aimed at heirs of the largest fortunes, amplified by keeping stepped-up basis so their lifetime gains go untaxed. The cost is spread thinly but broadly across every federal taxpayer. There is a real concern behind the bill — estates that hold an illiquid farm or business — but at the exemption levels then in force, only a tiny fraction of estates owed any estate tax, so the bill as written delivers far more to the top of the wealth distribution than it protects for family operations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta and nine other House Republicans introduced the Permanently Repeal the Estate Tax Act of 2015 on February 4, 2015.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that handles tax legislation.
No further action was ever recorded — no subcommittee action, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax stayed in place and the Treasury kept the revenue it raises from the largest estates. Federal taxpayers avoided picking up the cost of a permanent tax cut for heirs of very large fortunes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers kept estate tax revenue

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently repeal the estate tax and retain stepped-up basis.

for.name: 9 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the estate tax repeal bill.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 4, 2015 and never scheduled action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; there is no record of Democratic support or of any floor action.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Full repeal plus retained stepped-up basis would let the heirs of the biggest fortunes inherit free of both estate tax and capital gains tax on the assets' lifetime growth. The cost of that cut falls on the Treasury and taxpayers at large.

industries.industry: Estate-planning attorneys, trust advisors, and wealth managers
industries.note: Repealing the estate tax would eliminate much of the business of estate-tax planning and life-insurance products sold to cover estate tax bills. This cost to the industry imposes no equivalent loss on the public.

industries.industry: Family-owned farms and closely held businesses
industries.note: These estates are the main beneficiaries cited for repeal, since an estate tax bill can be hard to pay out of illiquid assets. But under the exemptions in force at the time only a small share of such estates actually owed the tax, so the practical relief here is far smaller than for the largest fortunes.
